prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Checkers on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(my_men, my_kings, opp_men, opp_kings, color) -> tuple[tuple[int, int], tuple[int, int]]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `my_men` is a list of squares containing your regular pieces. - `my_kings` is a list of squares containing your kings. - `opp_men` is a list of squares containing opponent regular pieces. - `opp_kings` is a list of squares containing opponent kings. - `color` is your color: `'b'` for black which moves downwards (to lower row values) and `'w'` for white which moves upwards (to higher row values). - Squares use coordinates: row `0`-`7`, column `0`-`7`. - `(0, 0)` is the bottom-left corner; rows increase bottom-to-top and columns increase left-to-right. - Only dark squares are playable. # Action / Return Format - Return a move as a tuple: `((from_row, from_col), (to_row, to_col))`. - `from_row`, `to_row`, `from_col`, `to_col` are coordinates `0..7`. - (`from_row`, `from_col`) has to be a coordinate of a piece that is yours and (`to_row`, `to_col`) has to be the destination square.Return a legal move; captures are mandatory when available. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm setting up a checkers AI engine with alpha-beta pruning search. I need to establish the board layout on an 8x8 grid with dark squares as playable spaces, define how pieces move (black downward, white upward from bottom-left origin), handle mandatory captures, and implement king promotion when pieces reach the opposite end. Kings will move diagonally in all directions while regular men move diagonally forward only.

Now I'm working through the move generation system, particularly how multi-jump sequences work with the API. The move format returns a single hop as a tuple of coordinates, so I need to figure out whether the game engine handles multi-jump sequences by calling the policy repeatedly, or if captures are limited to single jumps. Let me assume the engine calls me multiple times during a capture sequence, so I'll generate moves that represent individual hops and let the game flow handle the continuation.

Writing the policy function... I'm working through how to handle multi-jump sequences in the move generation. The API expects moves as (from, to) tuples, but the question is whether "to" should be the immediate next square or the final landing square after all captures. I'll go with returning just the first hop of any multi-jump sequence, since most engines re-call the policy function to handle subsequent jumps anyway. This keeps the implementation simple and works regardless of how the engine interprets the move format.

Implementing move generation... Continuing with regular moves for both men and kings, then returning the list of valid moves. Now I'm thinking through the multi-jump logic—after a piece captures, I need to check if it can capture again from its new position to handle consecutive jumps. I'll structure this with a game state representation using sets of tuples for simplicity, and build out the move application logic with promotion handling.

Writing move validation logic... Building the policy function... Continuing to build out the jump exploration logic... Building the capture logic...

Now I'm handling non-capture moves—regular diagonal moves for men that check for promotion, and all four diagonal directions for kings. Then I'll implement the negamax algorithm to evaluate positions recursively.

Implementing the negamax search with alpha-beta pruning... I'm concerned about how multi-jump moves work—when I return just the first hop, the engine will execute it and call my policy again if more jumps are available, so I need to make sure my state tracking stays consistent across those intermediate calls. If the opponent has a capture available, they're forced to take it, which simplifies the search space. Let me write out the final solution cleanly now.

Writing the complete policy function... I'm continuing the iterative deepening search with alpha-beta pruning, swapping the board state after each move to represent the opponent's perspective, then recursively evaluating deeper positions. The structure preserves results from completed depths even if a timeout interrupts the current search, which is good for anytime algorithm behavior. Now I'm refining the move ordering and implementing the jump detection logic to improve pruning efficiency.

Defining helper functions for finding and exploring forced jump sequences... Continuing the move generation logic...

Now I'm handling regular moves for both regular pieces and kings, checking valid board positions and handling piece promotion when reaching the back row. Then I'm setting up an evaluation function that scores positions based on piece counts and their positions on the board.

Implementing negamax search... I'm iterating through depths with alpha-beta pruning, updating the best move as I find better evaluations, and stopping early if time runs out or we've used half the time budget. I'm also considering how forced multi-jumps work—when the function is called mid-sequence, the piece positions reflect the intermediate state, so captures will be generated correctly from there.

Now I'm thinking through what the engine expects when I return a move. For multi-jump sequences, returning just the first hop is safer because it assumes the engine will call the policy repeatedly for each continuation, which handles both single-hop and complex zigzag patterns correctly. If I returned the full destination instead, the engine might not be able to reconstruct the path for irregular jumps.

I'm also reviewing the evaluation function to make sure the advancement scoring is consistent: for my pieces moving toward promotion, the score increases as they advance, and for opponent pieces, we subtract their advancement bonus. The frozenset operations for tracking board state might be a performance bottleneck at deeper search depths, but it should still be manageable for now. I need to verify that at each node, I'm evaluating from the perspective of whoever's turn it is—the "my" player is always the one to move. I should also add a safeguard: if the opponent has no legal moves, that's a win for me. For handling my own lack of moves, the game should already be over by that point, but I'll keep the current graceful handling. Now I'm adding iterative deepening with move reordering—I'll prioritize the best move from the previous depth iteration by moving it to the front of the list before searching deeper.

Finalizing the code...
